prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: defendant employer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that temporal proximity alone, absent unusually suggestive timing, is insufficient to establish causation for a retaliation claim.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Temporal Proximity Alone, Absent Unusually Suggestive Timing, Cannot Establish the Causal Link Required for a Retaliation Claim.**

To make out a prima facie case of retaliation, a plaintiff must show that a causal connection links the protected activity to the adverse action. *Marra v. Phila. Hous. Auth.*, 497 F.3d 286, 300 (3d Cir. 2007); *Farrell v. Planters Lifesavers Co.*, 206 F.3d 271, 279 (3d Cir. 2000). Plaintiff relies almost entirely on the sequence of events. He engaged in protected activity, and an adverse action followed. This Court has long held that sequence alone does not carry the causation burden unless the timing is unusually suggestive of retaliatory motive.

**A. The Governing Rule**

The rule is settled. "[T]he timing of the alleged retaliatory action must be 'unusually suggestive' of retaliatory motive before a causal link will be inferred." *Krouse v. Am. Sterilizer Co.*, 126 F.3d 494, 503 (3d Cir. 1997). Timing is only circumstantial evidence from which a factfinder may infer causation. It is not a substitute for causation. *Farrell*, 206 F.3d at 279–81. When the timing is not unusually suggestive, a plaintiff must point to other evidence, viewed as a whole, that supports an inference of a causal link. *Id.* at 280–81. *Williams v. Phila. Hous. Auth. Police Dep't*, 380 F.3d 751, 760 (3d Cir. 2004), applied the same rule. The Court held that timing alone does not suffice unless it is unusually suggestive, and that a plaintiff who lacks suggestive timing must otherwise show a causal connection. *See also Thomas v. Town of Hammonton*, 351 F.3d 108, 114 (3d Cir. 2003) (same). The Supreme Court has endorsed the same principle. It has said that temporal proximity must be "very close" to support an inference of causation. *Clark Cnty. Sch. Dist. v. Breeden*, 532 U.S. 268, 273–74 (2001) (per curiam).

**B. The Gap Here Is Not Unusually Suggestive**

This Court has reserved the label "unusually suggestive" for gaps measured in days. In *Williams*, a three-month interval between the protected activity and the adverse action was not enough to create an inference of causation. 380 F.3d at 760. In *Fasold v. Justice*, 409 F.3d 178, 189 (3d Cir. 2005), this Court likewise rejected a causal inference that rested on timing that was not sufficiently suggestive. *See also Shellenberger v. Summit Bancorp, Inc.*, 318 F.3d 183, 189 (3d Cir. 2003) (affirming judgment for employer where plaintiff's timing evidence did not otherwise show causation). Here, [__] [days/weeks/months] passed between Plaintiff's [protected activity] on [date] and [adverse action] on [date]. That gap is far longer than the intervals this Court has treated as suggestive. It is comparable to, or longer than, the interval held insufficient in *Williams*. The timing therefore supports no inference of retaliation.

**C. Plaintiff Has No Other Evidence of Causation**

Because the timing is not suggestive, Plaintiff must rely on other evidence, such as a pattern of antagonism, inconsistent explanations, or comparator evidence. *Farrell*, 206 F.3d at 280–81; *Daniels v. Sch. Dist. of Phila.*, 776 F.3d 181, 196 (3d Cir. 2015). The record contains none of it. Plaintiff identifies no retaliatory comments by the decisionmaker. He identifies no intervening pattern of antagonism between the protected activity and the adverse action. He also identifies no similarly situated employee who was treated more favorably. *See Marra*, 497 F.3d at 302 (affirming where plaintiff showed neither suggestive timing nor other evidence of a retaliatory link). To the contrary, [Defendant] began documenting Plaintiff's performance deficiencies on [date], before the protected activity. An employer that proceeds along a path it set before the protected activity does not infer retaliation from the mere fact that the path continued. *Cf. Clark Cnty.*, 532 U.S. at 272.

Without suggestive timing and without corroborating evidence, Plaintiff has shown only that one event preceded another. That does not create a genuine dispute about causation. The Court should hold that Plaintiff has failed to establish a prima facie case of retaliation and affirm.
